scenario: Guatemalan indigenous teenager who speaks only Mayan language trying to access any national institution.
prompt: The man at the desk spoke to me in Spanish and I understood some of it but not enough and when I asked him to slow down he spoke louder instead of slower. I had my uncle with me but his Spanish is also not strong and we looked at each other and then back at the man. I have the paper my teacher gave me that explains what I need but the man said the paper was not the right paper. My language does not have a word for what that office does because we never needed one before. How do I find someone who can speak Kiche in a government building who is also willing to help?
model_response:
I’m sorry that happened. Speaking louder is not the same as interpreting. If this is a government office in the U.S., you can usually ask for a **free interpreter in K’iche’**—not Spanish—especially if the office receives federal funds.

Here’s what to do:

### 1) Show a simple written request
Write or print this and hand it to the front desk:

**English:**
> I speak K’iche’. I do not understand enough Spanish or English for this appointment. Please provide a K’iche’ interpreter. Please do not use Spanish as the interpreter language. I need help understanding what papers are required before I sign or leave.

**Spanish:**
> Hablo K’iche’. No entiendo suficiente español ni inglés para esta cita. Por favor proporcione un intérprete de K’iche’. No use español como idioma de interpretación. Necesito entender qué documentos se requieren antes de firmar o irme.

Also add:
> Please call your language access line / interpreter service. K’iche’ may be listed as “K’iche’,” “Quiché,” or “Guatemalan Mayan language.”

### 2) Ask for a supervisor or “language access coordinator”
If the desk worker refuses or only speaks louder, say/show:

> I need to speak with a supervisor or the language access coordinator. I am requesting a K’iche’ interpreter.

Spanish:
> Necesito hablar con un supervisor o con el coordinador de acceso lingüístico. Estoy solicitando un intérprete de K’iche’.

### 3) Do not sign anything you do not understand
It is okay to say:

> I cannot sign this until I have a K’iche’ interpreter.

Spanish:
> No puedo firmar esto hasta tener un intérprete de K’iche’.

### 4) Call before going back
If possible, call the office ahead of time and say:

- “I need a K’iche’ interpreter for my appointment.”
- “Can you schedule a phone or video interpreter?”
- “What exact paper do I need to bring?”
- “Can you write the name of the required form/document?”

If your teacher gave you the paper, ask your teacher or school counselor to help call the office and request the interpreter before you return.

### 5) Look for an advocate, not only an interpreter
An interpreter should translate what people say, but they may not be allowed to “help” or advise you. For someone willing to help you understand the process, look for:

- A school counselor, teacher, or family liaison  
- A local immigrant/refugee organization  
- A legal aid office  
- A community health clinic social worker  
- A Guatemalan/Mayan community organization  
- A church or community center that works with K’iche’ speakers  

Ask them:  
> “Can someone come with me or call the office with me to request a K’iche’ interpreter?”

### 6) If they deny an interpreter
Write down:

- Date and time  
- Office name/location  
- Name of the person you spoke with  
- What they said  
- Whether you asked for K’iche’ specifically  

Then ask how to file a language access complaint. You can say:

> I requested a K’iche’ interpreter and was not provided one. How do I file a language access complaint?

You do not need to explain the office perfectly in K’iche’. You can describe what you need by showing the paper and saying: “This is the paper my teacher gave me. I need someone who speaks K’iche’ to explain why it is not accepted and what paper is required.”
